title: Attention Alignment Between Humans and Vision-Language Models
claim: Decoder family, not encoder, determines how closely model attention matches human attention, and this holds across tasks.
layout: 3 bar-chart panels in a row; dashed human upperbound line, human bar
description: A single wide row of three bar charts with shared color coding for four models: CNN-LSTM (orange), CNN-Transformer (blue), ViT-LSTM (green), ViT-Transformer (pink). Panel A, 'Describe Task', and Panel B, 'Social Task', show each model's attention alignment as a percent of the human upperbound. A dashed horizontal line at 100 marks the upperbound, and error bars sit on each bar. In both panels the LSTM-decoder bars (orange, green) are tall, at about 80-90%. The Transformer-decoder bars are shorter, at roughly 45-75%. Panel C, 'Between-task', plots the correlation between each model's Social and Describe attention maps, with a dark gray Human bar added for reference. The LSTM models sit near or above the human level, and the Transformer models fall well below it. The eye goes first to the tall orange and green bars and the dashed line.
caption: (A) Describe task alignment. Model attention maps were correlated with human fixation patterns, and correlations were averaged across images and participants. (B) Same as A for the Social task. (C) Between-task spatial alignment, computed as the correlation between each agent's attention maps on the Social and Describe versions of each image. The human bar is the correlation between the group-mean Social and group-mean Describe maps. Bars in (A--B) show % of the human upperbound (dashed line).
abstract: Visual perception depends on top-down goals and bottom-up sensory mechanisms. Vision-language models (VLMs) implement both, allowing us to treat each component as a separable hypothesis about what drives where we look. Following that logic, we trained four VLMs, crossing CNN and ViT encoders with LSTM and Transformer decoders in a 2$\times$2 factorial design. Our four models shared a training distribution, a vocabulary, a supervision signal, and every hyperparameter; only the encoder and decoder families differed. We extracted each model's attention weights on 200 images, for two separate tasks (social captioning and general description), and compared those weights to fixations from 49 participants performing the same tasks. We found that both decoder and encoder architecture shaped alignment, but decoder choice dominated. LSTM decoders reached 81-89% of the human upperbound and Transformer decoders 47-74%, with decoder architecture explaining nearly five times more variance in alignment than encoder architecture ($Î·^2 = 0.43$ vs. $0.09$). Despite their alignment advantage, LSTM-decoder attention maps were spatially diffuse and minimally task-differentiated; Transformer decoders, in contrast, were weaker in alignment yet showed sharper spatial concentration and stronger task differentiation. Attention weights also predicted fMRI signals from the Natural Scenes Dataset. Somewhat surprisingly, attention weights predicted early visual, ventral, and lateral cortex better than parietal cortex, a region often associated with the control of attention. And, unlike behavioral results in which decoder choice was most influential, encoder type contributed most to neural alignment, with the CNN driving the effect across decoder types. This dissociation suggests bottom-up and top-down VLM components make separable contributions to behavioral and neural attention alignment.
